details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Lidia is a web app that brings together the health of a crew on Mars and the Perseverance rover mission in a single 3D environment. It is live at lidia-silk.vercel.app.

Lidia has two parts, reached from a start lobby.

1. Health (Lidia · Body). A health monitor for a crew on Mars.

  • 3D body: an interactive human figure with organs, bones, muscles and body systems. Each organ is colored by its status: normal, watch or act.
  • Indicators: blood pressure, heart rate, heart rate variability, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood, with 30-day charts and a “Today” panel.
  • The user's real data: a WHOOP band via OAuth, live pulse over Bluetooth from the browser, and a pulse reading with the phone camera.
  • Lab reports: you upload a PDF or a photo of a lab test. Google Gemini reads the values, you review and correct them, and Lidia saves them to each crew member's medical record. Those values update the indicators and alerts.
  • Onboard agent: detects out-of-range values and suggests careful actions, such as “discuss it with the flight surgeon.”
  • “Ask Lidia”: answers by text or voice using only the crew member's data. It checks every figure it cites against its sources. It does not diagnose or prescribe.
  • Routine and gamification to keep up healthy habits.

2. Rover. A 3D simulator of the Perseverance rover in Jezero Crater.

  • Terrain built from HiRISE, CTX and MOLA elevation models and orbital imagery.
  • The rover's real traverse, from NASA's MMGIS waypoints.
  • Raw images from Mastcam and the Ingenuity helicopter, panoramas and rocks of scientific interest.
  • Day/night cycle, dust, Mars time (sols) and mission telemetry.

What benefits does it offer?

  • It gathers data that is usually scattered — wearables, manual readings and lab tests — into one view, shown on the body in a visual, easy-to-read way.
  • It helps spot trends early: it warns when a value drifts out of range before the problem grows. This matters on long missions, where the doctor is far away and communications are delayed.
  • It is educational: it explains what each indicator means and why it changes in space, such as bone loss or fluid shifts in microgravity.
  • It brings Mars exploration closer to the public with real NASA data in a 3D world you can explore.

What is the intended impact?

  • In space: a prototype of how a crew could monitor its own health autonomously on missions to the Moon or Mars, with an assistant that interprets the data without replacing the flight surgeon.
  • On Earth: the same approach serves people in remote places (Antarctic bases, offshore platforms, rural areas) and anyone who wants to understand their own health data and lab results.
  • In education: sparking interest in science, space medicine and planetary exploration among students and the general public.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Area

What we used

Languages

JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML and CSS

3D and graphics

Three.js with glTF/Draco models and Web Workers; Apache ECharts for the 30-day charts

Build and server

Vite for development; Node.js serverless functions deployed on Vercel

AI

Google Gemini: reads lab reports from PDF or photo, answers questions and transcribes voice

Browser APIs

Web Bluetooth (live pulse), camera (pulse), voice, IndexedDB and localStorage

Hardware

WHOOP band (OAuth API and Bluetooth), phone camera, computer or phone

NASA data

HiRISE, CTX, MOLA, Mars 2020 in MMGIS, Perseverance and Ingenuity raw images, Jezero science data

Human models

MakeHuman (CC0 license)

Quality

174 automated tests with Playwright

Code

GitHub

How is it creative?

  • It joins the astronaut's health and the mission around them in one project: the crew's bodies and the rover on Mars.
  • Health is shown on a 3D human body instead of in tables. A high-cholesterol result, for example, lights up the heart.
  • It turns a lab PDF into a structured medical record with AI, but the person always reviews it before saving.
  • The assistant checks its own figures against the data before answering, so it does not make up numbers.
  • It mixes real data from a consumer wearable with a fictional crew, so anyone can try it with their own body (“You”).

What factors did the team consider?

  • Safety and medical ethics: it is an educational tool, not a medical device, and says so on screen. It does not diagnose or prescribe, and always refers to a professional.
  • Privacy: the medical record and health data are stored only in the user's browser. Reports are sent to Gemini only to read them, with a notice beforehand. API keys never reach the browser.
  • Data reliability: the lab's own reference ranges take priority. If the report has none, general ranges are used (MedlinePlus/NIH, ADA, AHA). Estimated metrics are labeled “educational estimates.”
  • Real mission conditions: communication delays, crew autonomy and unstable connections. For example, the Bluetooth band resumes measuring on its own when you put it back on.
  • Scientific rigor: data and terrain from official NASA sources.
  • Accessibility and performance: it works on phones and computers. The 3D body is cached so it loads instantly. It supports voice input and is in Spanish.
